description.text: Particles can be emitted on one or more channels; only particles on the selected channels will have this force applied to them.
color

When this option is turned on, the mass of any spawned particles will be removed from the originating particle. If the mass of the originating particle is zero at the end of a frame, it will be deleted.
When this option is turned on, the momentum of any spawned particles will be subtracted from the momentum of the originating particle, in correspondence with Newton's third law of motion.
How to draw in 3D preview.  The viewer can override this setting.

Identifies the channels that the particles will be in. By default, the particles from the spawn are present in the B channel only. You can have multiple emitters emitting particles into different channels, and particle force nodes affecting different channels.
Allows you to import transformation data from an external file or export existing transformation data to an external file
Transform Data

This determines whether the particle representations animate after emission.  If "constant", then they do not animate, and keep the same representation for their entire lifetime.  If "in steps", then the representation advances frame by frame.  If "randomly", then a different random frame is picked each time.

Setting a half-life will make a fraction of particles die randomly each frame such that on average half of the particles that existed at a given time will continue to exist after the half-life (as per radioactive decay). After twice this time, only a quarter of the original particles will be left, etc.
If this is set the particle color will be taken from the originating particle.  Otherwise it will come from the color knob.

This knob determines which "particles" input will be used for the representation. If it is "randomly", then a random input will be picked for each particle.  Otherwise, if it is "in order", the inputs will be cycled through.
The number of frames that each particle will exist for.

Produces a random variation in the max lifetime value. Adds a Gaussian-distributed random number to the value multiplied by the variation value. Roughly, setting variation to 1 produces random numbers between 0 and  2*value, with a bell-shaped distribution around "value" 
0 means it's the number it's meant to be, 1 means it's very random.
Each particle has a mass which only comes into play when a force is applied.

Produces a random variation in the mass value. Adds a Gaussian-distributed random number to the value multiplied by the variation value. Roughly, setting variation to 1 produces random numbers between 0 and  2*value, with a bell-shaped distribution around "value" 
0 means it's the number it's meant to be, 1 means it's very random.

The number of frames that will be used in animation from the particle input.
This node only applies to particles which are above this age, where the age is normalised to 0-1.

The probability that any given particle will be affected by this op.
For each incoming particle, the op generates a random number between 0 and 1 and if that number is greater than "probability", it ignores the particle and leaves it unchanged.

0.0 = never affects any particles.
1.0 = affects every particle.

The number of particles emitted per particle per frame. It is an exact number, not an average. It will decrease if you change the probability. It is affected by the setting of the rate channel: if your rate channel is not at a value of 1 all the way through, the emission rate would be less.

Produces a random variation in the emission rate value. Adds a Gaussian-distributed random number to the value multiplied by the variation value. Roughly, setting variation to 1 produces random numbers between 0 and  2*value, with a bell-shaped distribution around "value" 
0 means it's the number it's meant to be, 1 means it's very random.
The shape within which particles will be affected by this op.
If checked, particles outside the region will be affected rather than those inside it.
Sets how the object will render.  Independent from the OpenGL preview selection.
Specifies the order to apply Euler angles to the rotation.
Rotate

Particles have an orientation in 3D space and they spin around their local y-axis according to the rotation velocity. 
The y-axis points in the direction the particles were initially emitted, but then stays unchanged although there is (will be soon) a node which will align particles along their direction of motion.

Produces a random variation in the rotation velocity value. Adds a Gaussian-distributed random number to the value multiplied by the variation value. Roughly, setting variation to 1 produces random numbers between 0 and  2*value, with a bell-shaped distribution around "value" 
0 means it's the number it's meant to be, 1 means it's very random.
Scale

Used for anything that needs random numbers, in particular the probability. Its also used for things like the 'range' knobs in the emitter. You can achieve slightly different effects by changing the seed number.
Turn off to prevent picking with the mouse in the viewer.
The size of each particle. If the 'particle' input is geometry, the instance of that geometry at each particle will be affected by this value.

Produces a random variation in the size value. Adds a Gaussian-distributed random number to the value multiplied by the variation value. Roughly, setting variation to 1 produces random numbers between 0 and  2*value, with a bell-shaped distribution around "value"
0 means it's the number it's meant to be, 1 means it's very random.
Skew

Set your geometry or pivot location to that of a selection within the scene
  • Geo to selection (position): sets the position of your geometry to the selection within the scene
  • Geo to selection (position, orientation): sets the position and orientation of your geometry to the selection within the scene
  • Geo to selection (position, orientation, size): sets the position, orientation and size of your geometry to the selection within the scene
  • Pivot to selection (position): sets the pivot position to the selection within the scene
  • Pivot to selection (orientation): sets the pivot orientation to the selection within the scene
  • Pivot to selection (position, orientation): sets the pivot position and orientation to the selection within the scene
Snap
Applies a spread to the particles. By default it forms a cone shape around the normal of each emission point.

This knob determines the frame at which a newly emitted particle's representation starts from the selected input. If "first", it picks the first frame from the input for each new particle. If "in order", it picks successive frames for each new particle. If "current", it picks the frame that the particle was emitted. If "random", it picks a random frame within the representation's frame range.

This forces particle start frames to be within the range of the representation input, causing the "in order" and "current" options to wrap round back to the start of the frame range once it has been exceeded, in a loop.If the input is geometry with an animated texture, then you may need to add a FrameRange node as the default frame range for geometry is 1-1.
Transfers any velocity that the initial emitter has to the particles.
